title: Myrkl Review: Does It Work? vs ZBiotics, vs Cheers, Side Effects
excerpt: An honest Myrkl review: how the alcohol-eating probiotic pill is supposed to work, what its one small study shows, Reddit sentiment, side effects, and how it compares with ZBiotics and Cheers.
metaDescription: Does Myrkl work? An honest review of the probiotic pre-drinking pill: science, side effects, Reddit sentiment, and how it compares to ZBiotics and Cheers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Myrkl is a real product from a real company with an interesting pitch: a probiotic pill whose bacteria are meant to start breaking down alcohol in your gut before it reaches your bloodstream. It has more published human research than most hangover products, which is to its credit. But that research is one small, company-funded trial that measured blood alcohol, not how people felt the next morning. There is no good evidence yet that Myrkl makes hangovers noticeably better for most people, and the theory has a built-in limit, because most alcohol is absorbed quickly and processed in the liver, where gut bacteria can't reach.

**The quick verdict:** Myrkl looks low risk for most healthy adults and isn't a scam, but it's a speculative purchase. Some users say they feel clearer the next day. Many others, including plenty of people on Reddit, say they noticed nothing. If you want to try it, go in with modest expectations and never use it to judge whether you're fine to drive. If you want the hangover option with the broadest research behind it for the money, Myrkl isn't the obvious first pick.

> **This is not medical advice.** This review explains published research and how the company describes its own product. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Myrkl is sold as a food supplement, not a medicine. It is not approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and it does not make you sober, make it safe to drive, or protect you from alcohol poisoning. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist first if** you have a weakened immune system (from chemotherapy, an organ transplant, HIV, or immune-suppressing drugs), a central IV line, a damaged heart valve, a history of pancreatitis, a serious digestive condition, or you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or take prescription medicine. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, pale or bluish skin, or being hard to wake, call 911 right away.

## What Is Myrkl?

Myrkl is a "pre-drinking" supplement made by De Faire Medical, a company based in Sweden. It launched in the UK in 2022 and got a burst of media attention, with headlines describing a pill that "eats" alcohol before it can get you drunk. It has since become available in other markets, including the US, and is usually sold online in packs of capsules.

The name and the marketing are clever, and that's part of why it gets searched so much. The core idea is different from most hangover products. Instead of trying to ease symptoms the morning after, or support your liver while it works, Myrkl aims to reduce how much alcohol you absorb in the first place.

### What's in Myrkl

According to the company's descriptions, Myrkl contains a blend of probiotic bacteria (live microbes, here chosen because they are said to break down alcohol), along with an amino acid and a B vitamin. Different sources and pack versions have listed the strains differently over the years, with *Bacillus* species featuring prominently in the company's materials, so the most reliable thing to do is read the current label on the pack you're buying. Bacteria from the *Bacillus* group are common in probiotic products because they form hardy spores that survive stomach acid better than many other microbes.

What Myrkl doesn't contain is worth noting too. It has no DHM (dihydromyricetin, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol and the brain), no pain reliever, no caffeine, and no electrolytes. It is a single-mechanism product built around the bacteria.

### How you're meant to take it

Myrkl is designed to be taken **before** drinking, not after. The company's instructions have described taking capsules a set number of hours ahead of your first drink, and the main trial pre-dosed participants for about a week before the drinking session. Follow whatever the current label says. The key point is simple: Myrkl is not a morning-after remedy. If you wake up with a hangover, taking it then is unlikely to help, because the alcohol it was supposed to intercept is already long gone from your gut.

## How Myrkl Is Supposed to Work

To judge Myrkl fairly, it helps to understand the basic chemistry of what happens when you drink.

When you swallow a drink, the alcohol (ethanol) passes through your stomach and into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed into your bloodstream. From there, it travels to your liver. Your liver uses an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase to turn ethanol into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic chemical that contributes to flushing, nausea and some hangover symptoms. A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, then converts acetaldehyde into acetate, which is mostly harmless.

Myrkl's pitch is to get in front of this process. If the bacteria in the capsule break down some of the alcohol while it's still in your gut, less of it reaches your blood. Less alcohol in your blood, in theory, means less intoxication and less for your liver to process overnight.

That's a coherent idea, and it's not pseudoscience. Some bacteria genuinely can metabolize alcohol. The open questions are about scale and timing.

### The problem of speed

Alcohol is absorbed fast. On an empty stomach, a large share of a drink can reach your bloodstream within roughly half an hour to an hour, which is why you feel a drink fairly quickly. For Myrkl to make a real difference, the bacteria would need to break down a meaningful amount of alcohol in the short window before your intestine absorbs it. That's a tall order, especially when you're drinking a lot or drinking quickly.

### The problem of where alcohol is processed

Most alcohol metabolism happens in your liver, not your gut. A bacterium working in your intestines can only act on the alcohol that's still sitting there. Once alcohol is in your blood, Myrkl has no way of touching it.

### The acetaldehyde question

There's also a subtle catch. If gut bacteria break down alcohol, the first step usually produces acetaldehyde, the same toxic chemical your liver makes. Making acetaldehyde in the gut rather than the liver is not automatically better for you, and gut acetaldehyde is something researchers have raised concerns about in its own right. Whether this matters in practice with Myrkl isn't clear, but it's a fair question that the marketing tends to skip.

## What the Myrkl Evidence Actually Shows

The main study behind Myrkl is a small randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in the journal *Nutrition and Metabolic Insights*. It involved roughly two dozen healthy adults and was funded by the company. Participants took the supplement or a placebo for about a week, then drank a moderate, measured amount of alcohol, and the researchers tracked their blood alcohol over the following hours. They reported substantially lower blood alcohol levels with the supplement compared with placebo.

That's a genuinely interesting result, and having any published human trial puts Myrkl ahead of many hangover products that have none. But it's important to be clear about what this study did and didn't show.

**What it showed:**
- In a small group of healthy adults, under controlled conditions, blood alcohol readings were lower after taking the supplement for a week.

**What it didn't show:**
- It didn't measure whether people felt less hungover the next day, which is the reason most buyers are interested.
- It didn't test a typical night out with heavy or fast drinking, varied drinks, or food.
- It hasn't been repeated in larger, independent trials run by researchers with no stake in the result.
- It used a week of pre-dosing, which is different from swallowing a couple of capsules an hour before a party.

Small company-funded studies aren't worthless, but they're the first step, not the final word. Positive early results often shrink or disappear when larger independent trials are run. Until that happens, the honest summary is that Myrkl has an intriguing early finding about blood alcohol and no good evidence that it reliably reduces hangovers.

### What experts said at launch

When Myrkl launched in the UK, several independent experts quoted in the British press raised the same points covered above: the small study size, the industry funding, the speed of alcohol absorption, and the fact that most metabolism happens in the liver. A recurring concern was behavioral. A pill that promises to lower your blood alcohol could encourage people to drink more, or lead them to believe they're less impaired than they are. That's a fair worry, and it's the most important safety point in this review.

## Does Myrkl Work? What Users and Reddit Say

User feedback on Myrkl is mixed, which is typical for hangover products.

**The positive reports** usually come from people who drink moderately. They say they woke up clearer, slept better, or felt "less rough" than usual after a few drinks. Some say they felt the effects of alcohol a little less during the evening.

**The negative and neutral reports** are just as common. Many people on Reddit and in review sections say they couldn't tell any difference, especially after a heavier night. Some point out that they also drank water, ate well, or drank less on the night they tried it, so it's hard to know what actually helped. A frequent complaint is price: once you work out the cost per night out, it adds up, and several people say they'd rather spend the money on a good meal and electrolytes.

There are a few honest reasons user reviews are hard to interpret:

- **Hangovers vary a lot from night to night** depending on how much you drank, how fast, whether you ate, how well you slept, and what you drank. One good morning proves very little.
- **The placebo effect is real.** If you've paid for something and expect it to help, you may feel better regardless.
- **People change their behavior.** Taking a pre-drinking supplement can make people more mindful, so they also pace themselves or drink more water.

So reviews that say "it worked for me" aren't lying, but they can't tell you whether Myrkl itself made the difference.

## Myrkl Side Effects and Safety

For most healthy adults, Myrkl appears to be low risk. The *Bacillus* group of bacteria is widely used in probiotic products, and side effects from probiotics are usually mild, such as gas, bloating, or a change in bowel habits for the first few days.

There are a few groups who should be more careful with any live-bacteria supplement:

- People with a weakened immune system, including those on chemotherapy, organ transplant recipients, and people on immune-suppressing drugs
- People with a central IV line or a damaged or artificial heart valve
- Anyone with a history of pancreatitis or a serious bowel condition
- People who are pregnant or breastfeeding, where data are limited

If any of these applies to you, talk to your doctor before trying Myrkl.

### The biggest risk isn't the pill

The real safety concern with Myrkl is how people use it. Please keep these points in mind:

- **It does not make you sober.** Even if it lowers your blood alcohol somewhat, you can still be well over the legal driving limit and seriously impaired.
- **Never use it to decide whether you can drive.** Don't drive after drinking, full stop.
- **It won't protect you from alcohol poisoning.** If you drink a dangerous amount, a probiotic won't save you.
- **Don't treat it as permission to drink more.** That cancels out any benefit and adds risk.

## Myrkl vs ZBiotics

Myrkl and ZBiotics get compared constantly because they're the two best-known "hangover probiotics." They're built on related ideas but target different steps.

**ZBiotics** is a drink made with a genetically engineered strain of *Bacillus subtilis* designed to produce an enzyme that breaks down **acetaldehyde** in your gut. You drink one bottle before your first drink. **Myrkl** is a capsule whose bacteria are meant to break down **alcohol itself** in your gut, before it's absorbed.

| | Myrkl | ZBiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **Format** | Capsules | Small liquid drink |
| **What it targets** | Alcohol in the gut | Acetaldehyde in the gut |
| **Bacteria** | Probiotic blend (per company; check label) | Engineered *Bacillus subtilis* |
| **When to take** | Ahead of drinking, per label | Before the first drink |
| **Published human evidence** | One small, company-funded trial on blood alcohol | Mainly company research; limited independent data |
| **Hangover symptoms tested?** | Not in the main trial | No strong independent trial |
| **Biggest limit** | Alcohol absorbs fast; most is processed in the liver | Most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, not the gut |

**Which is better?** Neither has strong independent proof that it improves hangovers, so there's no clear winner. Myrkl can point to a published human trial showing lower blood alcohol, which ZBiotics can't quite match for that specific outcome. ZBiotics has a longer track record in the US market and a larger base of user reviews. Both share the same core weakness: they work only in the gut, while your liver does most of the heavy lifting.

If you prefer a pill, Myrkl is more convenient. If you're comfortable with a drink and want the better-known US brand, ZBiotics is the more common choice. For a deeper look at the other side of this comparison, see our full [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review), and for an overview of the whole category, our guide to [hangover probiotics](/never-hungover/hangover-probiotics).

## Myrkl vs Cheers

Cheers is a different kind of product altogether. Its best-known product, Cheers Restore, is a capsule built around **DHM** plus L-cysteine (an amino acid) and a few supporting ingredients. Rather than trying to stop alcohol from being absorbed, DHM has been studied for how it affects the brain's response to alcohol and how the body processes alcohol after it's absorbed.

| | Myrkl | Cheers Restore |
|---|---|---|
| **Main ingredient** | Probiotic bacteria | DHM plus L-cysteine |
| **Approach** | Break down alcohol in the gut before absorption | Support the body after alcohol is absorbed |
| **When to take** | Ahead of drinking | While or after drinking, per label |
| **Evidence** | One small trial on blood alcohol | DHM research is mostly animal and lab work, with limited human data; L-cysteine has small early human studies |
| **Live bacteria?** | Yes | No |

**Which is better?** Again, neither is a proven hangover cure. The choice comes down to approach and timing. Myrkl must be taken ahead of time and acts only in the gut. Cheers can be taken during or after a night out and acts after absorption, which addresses Myrkl's biggest weakness: most alcohol gets into your blood anyway. On the other hand, the main DHM research in hangovers is mostly from animal studies, so it shouldn't be oversold either. Our [Cheers Restore review](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review) covers that product in detail, and our [ZBiotics vs Cheers comparison](/never-hungover/zbiotics-vs-cheers) is useful if you're weighing a probiotic against a DHM product.

One practical point: Cheers charges a premium for its brand. If DHM is the part you're interested in, plain DHM supplements contain the same main ingredient for considerably less.

## Is Myrkl Worth the Money?

Myrkl usually costs noticeably more per night out than a basic DHM supplement and is in the same general range as other premium hangover products. Prices change and vary by country and pack size, so check the current price per use before buying.

Here's a fair way to think about value:

- **You might consider it if** you drink moderately and occasionally, you're curious about the gut-based approach, the price doesn't bother you, and you understand it's an experiment rather than a guarantee.
- **You'll probably be disappointed if** you drink heavily, you expect it to stop you getting drunk, or you want a product with strong evidence behind it.
- **Skip it if** you have any of the health conditions listed in the safety section without first talking to a doctor, or if you're tempted to use it as a reason to drink more.

### Myrkl pros and cons

**Pros:**
- Has at least one published, placebo-controlled human trial, which many hangover products don't
- Uses bacteria common in probiotic products and appears low risk for most healthy adults
- Simple capsule format, easy to carry
- A genuinely different approach from symptom-relief products

**Cons:**
- The main trial was small, short, and funded by the company
- No good evidence that it improves how you feel the next day
- Must be taken ahead of drinking; no help once a hangover has started
- Acts only in the gut, while most alcohol is absorbed quickly and processed in the liver
- Can create a false sense of being less impaired
- Pricier per use than basic DHM supplements

## What Actually Helps With Hangovers

Whatever you decide about Myrkl, the basics still do more than any pill. The most reliable ways to feel better the next morning are drinking less, eating a proper meal before you start, spacing alcoholic drinks with water, choosing lighter drinks over dark spirits, and protecting your sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each of these in more detail.

If you want a supplement in the mix, it's worth comparing approaches rather than defaulting to whichever brand is in the news. Probiotics like Myrkl and ZBiotics work in the gut. Pain relievers such as the aspirin in Blowfish target the headache (see our [Blowfish review](/never-hungover/blowfish-hangover-review) for the stomach risks of mixing aspirin with alcohol). DHM works after absorption and is far cheaper per serving than most branded hangover products.

If you want to try DHM, a straightforward single-ingredient option is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), which provides 1,000 mg per serving at a low cost per use. Like everything in this category, there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and the human research is still limited. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it, and you should check with a pharmacist first if you take sedatives, sleep aids, or other prescription medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Myrkl takes a real piece of biology and turns it into a product: bacteria that can break down alcohol, delivered as a capsule you take before drinking. It's more honest science than many hangover products can claim, with a published human trial showing lower blood alcohol in a small group of people. But that trial was small and company-funded, it didn't measure hangovers, and the approach is limited by how fast alcohol is absorbed and how much of it is processed in the liver. User reviews are split between people who feel a little better and people who notice nothing.

Compared with ZBiotics, it's a similar bet with a different target. Compared with Cheers, it works at a different stage, and DHM-based options cost less per night. If you try Myrkl, treat it as an experiment, keep drinking sensibly, and never let it change your decision about driving.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Myrkl actually work?**

Myrkl has one small, company-funded trial showing lower blood alcohol levels in healthy adults who took it for about a week before drinking a moderate amount. That's an interesting finding, but the study didn't measure hangover symptoms, and it hasn't been confirmed in larger independent trials. There is no good evidence yet that Myrkl reliably makes hangovers better. Some users report feeling better, while many notice no difference.

**What are the ingredients in Myrkl?**

The company describes Myrkl as a blend of probiotic bacteria, with *Bacillus* species prominent in its materials, plus an amino acid and a B vitamin. Strain listings have varied between sources and pack versions, so check the current label on the product you buy. Myrkl does not contain DHM, pain relievers, caffeine, or electrolytes.

**Is Myrkl better than ZBiotics?**

Neither has strong independent evidence for reducing hangovers, so there's no clear winner. Myrkl targets alcohol itself in the gut and has a small published trial showing lower blood alcohol. ZBiotics uses an engineered bacterium to break down acetaldehyde in the gut and is the better-known brand in the US. Both act only in the gut, while most alcohol and acetaldehyde are processed in the liver.

**Myrkl vs Cheers: which should I choose?**

They take different approaches. Myrkl is a probiotic taken before drinking that aims to reduce alcohol absorption in the gut. Cheers Restore is built around DHM and L-cysteine and acts after alcohol is absorbed. Neither is a proven hangover cure. If you're mainly interested in DHM, plain DHM supplements cost less than branded blends.

**When should I take Myrkl?**

Follow the current label. Myrkl is designed to be taken ahead of drinking, and the main trial pre-dosed participants for about a week. It isn't a morning-after remedy, so taking it once you already have a hangover is unlikely to help.

**Does Myrkl make you less drunk or safe to drive?**

No. Even if it lowers blood alcohol somewhat, you can still be well over the legal limit and seriously impaired. Never use Myrkl, or any supplement, to judge whether you're fit to drive. It also won't protect you from alcohol poisoning.

**Does Myrkl have side effects?**

Most healthy adults seem to tolerate it well. Probiotics can cause mild gas, bloating, or changes in bowel habits for a few days. People with weakened immune systems, central IV lines, damaged heart valves, a history of pancreatitis, or serious bowel conditions, and people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, should talk to a doctor before taking any live-bacteria supplement.

**Is Myrkl a scam?**

No. It's a real product from a real company, and it has more published human research than many hangover products. The issue isn't that it's fake. It's that the evidence is early and small, it doesn't cover hangover symptoms, and the marketing can make the results sound stronger than they are.
